# OpenThinRDP: the documentation in one file

Source: https://github.com/OpenThinRdp/openthinrdp (main), release 0.2.15, built 2026-10-22. Every section below is one file of the repository.

<p align="center"><img src="docs/logo.png" alt="OpenThinRDP" width="480"></p>

<p align="center"><b>The free thin client OS for Windows Remote Desktop, RDS and VDI.<br>
RDP over UDP that keeps working where TCP freezes, and a whole fleet managed from one Windows window.</b></p>

<p align="center">
<a href="https://github.com/OpenThinRdp/openthinrdp/releases/latest"><b>⬇ Download the ISO (latest release)</b></a>
&nbsp;·&nbsp; <a href="#try-it-in-five-minutes">Try it live, nothing installed</a>
&nbsp;·&nbsp; <a href="https://openthinrdp.github.io/">Website</a>
</p>

<p align="center">
<img src="docs/screenshots/boot.png" alt="Boot menu: try it live or install" width="32%">
<img src="docs/screenshots/sign-in.png" alt="Sign-in form" width="32%">
<img src="docs/screenshots/settings.png" alt="Settings of the device" width="32%">
</p>

**Turn any PC or old thin client into a locked-down Remote Desktop kiosk in five minutes.** It boots straight into
a sign-in form and connects to Windows: through an RD Connection Broker to the user's desktop or VM, or straight to
a session host or any Windows PC, **on premises or in the cloud**. No licence per device, no management server, no
agent, no cloud service to depend on: a shared folder and a small Windows manager are all it takes.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Smooth on bad lines** | RDP over UDP: on a line losing half of the packets the desktop still runs at 19-21 frames per second, where TCP has already frozen ([numbers below](#rdp-over-udp-that-keeps-going-on-a-bad-line)) |
| **Zero-touch setup** | a new device needs a domain account and nothing else: it finds its management folder in the domain by itself ([how](docs/manager.md#settings--manager-language-and-local-copy)) |
| **The whole fleet in one window** | state of every device, central settings, signed updates with pilot devices and rollback, power on (Wake-on-LAN), restart, remote screen |
| **The Windows side too** | Health Center: brokers, Hyper-V hosts and cluster, VMs, DCs, DNS, SQL AlwaysOn and backups, with a plain sentence and a fix for each problem |
| **Any x86-64 hardware** | UEFI with Secure Boot or legacy BIOS, complete Debian 13 kernel and firmware, from 2 GB of RAM |
| **Open source** | GPLv3: free to use, and every copy stays open source; Debian underneath, every client script readable in `rootfs/opt/openthinrdp` |

> **In production every day.** OpenThinRDP runs the whole thin client fleet of the company it was built for:
> 14 Dell OptiPlex 3000 Thin Clients at desks, tills, a laboratory, weighing stations and a wall screen on Wi-Fi,
> on a Windows 11 VDI on Hyper-V behind two RD Connection Brokers. Every release reaches them through their
> management folder and installs while people work, applied when the session is over. FreeRDP security releases
> reach OpenThinRDP [within 7 days](SECURITY.md#freerdp-security-fixes); the ISO is tested in QEMU/KVM with Secure
> Boot at every release and the system tests run on every commit
> ([CI](https://github.com/OpenThinRdp/openthinrdp/actions/workflows/tests.yml)). What is in production, what is only
> tested and what does not exist yet: **[docs/status.md](docs/status.md)**.

> **Not openthinclient.** OpenThinRDP is a new, independent project, not affiliated with openthinclient: the names
> sound alike, nothing else is shared. openthinclient boots its devices over the network (PXE) from its management
> server; OpenThinRDP is installed on each device or runs live from a USB stick, needs no server and is built around
> RDP with FreeRDP's UDP transport.

## RDP over UDP that keeps going on a bad line

Over TCP, every lost packet stops the screen until it is sent again: a lossy Wi-Fi, a VPN or a faulty cable is
enough to freeze the remote desktop. Over UDP, Windows drops what is late and lowers the quality instead, and the
desktop keeps moving. Measured on a Windows 11 VDI with a full-screen load changing every pixel, frame rate counted
by the server, loss applied to every packet from the virtual machine:

| packets lost | over TCP | **OpenThinRDP over UDP** |
|---|---|---|
| 0% | | **15-21 fps** |
| 5% | 7-12 fps | |
| 10% | 6 fps | |
| 20% | 0.6 fps: the screen barely moves | |
| 30% | 0.2 fps: frozen | |
| 50% | | **19-21 fps**, as on a clean line |
| 60% | | **14-21 fps** |
| 70% | | **18-19 fps** |
| 80% | | 4 fps, then the tunnel gives up |

Empty cells were not measured: TCP was already frozen at 30%, and UDP at 50% ran as on a clean line. One
environment (Dell OptiPlex 3000 Thin Client, Windows 11 VDI on Hyper-V), loss emulated with netem:
[the method and the scripts](tests/udp-bench/README.md) to get your own numbers, and every step in
[docs/udp.md](docs/udp.md#on-a-lossy-line).

The UDP transport comes from our work in FreeRDP: we found and fixed what made it fail on lossy lines, and it was
merged upstream as [#13608](https://github.com/FreeRDP/FreeRDP/pull/13608). Upstream ships it switched off;
OpenThinRDP has it on, with `TRANSPORT=tcp` one setting away.

## Who it is for

- You publish desktops with **Windows Remote Desktop Services**: RD Connection Broker with session hosts or a
  Hyper-V VDI collection. Or there is no broker at all: each device connects to one Windows PC or server (set
  its name instead of the broker), e.g. a reception desk that works on the PC in the office. Devices outside the
  office go through the **RD Gateway** over HTTPS ([`RDP_GATEWAY`](docs/configuration.md#rd-gateway)) or their own
  **VPN**, WireGuard or OpenVPN ([`VPN`](docs/configuration.md#vpn)).
- Your desktops are **in the cloud**: an RDS deployment or Windows virtual machines in Azure, AWS, Google Cloud
  or with any provider, reached through the RD Gateway or a VPN, with UDP through a VPN
  ([details](docs/configuration.md#desktops-in-the-cloud)). Azure Virtual Desktop and Windows 365 are not supported
  yet (they need a Microsoft Entra ID sign-in).
- You have **x86-64 PCs or thin clients, new or old**: UEFI with or without Secure Boot, or a legacy BIOS, with the
  complete Debian kernel and firmware ([hardware](docs/hardware.md)), and want to keep them useful without a licence
  per device.
- You want to **try RDP over UDP** on real clients, or help bring it into FreeRDP.
- You need **screens that only show a web page**: hall TVs, dashboards, info points, production boards. The same
  system, no sign-in, the page chosen centrally ([see below](#screens-that-only-show-a-web-page)), so one image
  covers the whole fleet.

Not for you (yet): Citrix, VMware/Omnissa Horizon and other protocols (OpenThinRDP does RDP only), 32-bit only
PCs. ARM is experimental: an SD card image for the Raspberry Pi 4
([pre-release](https://github.com/OpenThinRdp/openthinrdp/releases/tag/rpi-test-1)), tested in QEMU emulation only,
not yet on a real board ([what to check](docs/arm.md)); the Pi 5 is not supported yet.

## Requirements

| | Minimum |
|---|---|
| Device | any 64-bit x86 PC or thin client, **UEFI** (Secure Boot supported, not required) **or legacy BIOS**: old office PCs and used thin clients are fine |
| Drivers | the complete Debian 13 kernel and every Debian firmware package: what runs Debian 13 runs OpenThinRDP |
| Memory | 2 GB of RAM |
| Storage | 8 GB to install it (eMMC, SSD or disk); nothing to try it live from a USB stick |
| Network | cable, Wi-Fi or a USB Ethernet adapter; WPA2/WPA3 personal or Enterprise, and 802.1X on the cable |
| TPM 2.0 | optional: with one, the device's secrets (management folder password, Wi-Fi key, SSH host keys) are kept encrypted in it ([security](docs/security.md)); without one it works the same |
| Windows side | an RD Connection Broker (RDS session hosts or a Hyper-V VDI collection), or any Windows PC or server that accepts Remote Desktop (Pro, Enterprise, Server), on premises or in any cloud |

Tested hardware and firmware settings: [docs/hardware.md](docs/hardware.md).

## Try it in five minutes

1. [Download `openthinrdp-<version>.iso`](https://github.com/OpenThinRdp/openthinrdp/releases/latest) and write it
   to a USB stick with any raw image writer (Rufus in DD mode, balenaEtcher, `dd`).
2. Boot the PC from the stick. The menu starts the **live system** by itself after 10 seconds: it runs from the
   stick and **never writes to the disk**.
3. With a network, when GitHub has a newer version than the ISO it asks whether to download it or to use the
   ISO's (no answer in 30 seconds: the newer one), so the ISO does not need downloading again for every release.
   Then the settings dialog opens: set the broker (or the name of a Windows PC) and the domain, save, sign in.
4. Like it? Restart and choose **Install**: it shows the disk it is going to erase and asks before writing
   anything (answer *Yes* to go on), then about three minutes. It installs on the **first internal disk**, never
   a USB disk (not even the installation stick). For rollouts, *Unattended install* skips the question.

What the device needs: [Requirements](#requirements). The whole path, from the USB stick to a managed fleet:
[getting started](docs/guides/getting-started.md).

## What it does

- **Remote desktop over UDP.** Windows sends the graphics (and USB, sound and camera) over UDP and adapts frame rate and quality to the line
  instead of queueing: smoother on busy servers, lossy Wi-Fi and VPNs. The image ships FreeRDP with the UDP
  transport switched on ([FreeRDP #13608](https://github.com/FreeRDP/FreeRDP/pull/13608), merged upstream, off there by default).
  Per device: `auto` (UDP, TCP when UDP is blocked), `udp` (UDP only) or `tcp`. In our 3-hour test with packet
  loss, bandwidth limits, network cuts and killed clients the session stayed on UDP the whole time
  ([results](https://github.com/FreeRDP/FreeRDP/pull/13608#issuecomment-6110587552)). See [docs/udp.md](docs/udp.md).
- **Sign-in form, then full screen remote desktop.** Boots in a few seconds with your logo, no desktop, no
  shell. Retries, fallback brokers, clear messages for "no network", "broker not reachable", "the virtual
  machine does not start", wrong password (never retried, so accounts are not locked). A virtual machine that is
  restarting or installing a Windows update gets "Waiting for Windows" (up to 20 minutes) instead of an error.
- **Reconnects by itself** after network drops, stops when the session is ended on purpose (sign out,
  disconnect, VM shut down by an administrator), and warns before taking over a session open on another device.
  A session taken over by another device shows "Session opened elsewhere" with *Resume here*.
- **USB done right for VDI.** Signature keys, tachograph keys and other special devices go to Windows as whole
  USB devices, also when plugged in during the session. **Webcams and headsets work in meetings**: the camera goes
  through the RDP camera channel and the microphone through the RDP audio channel, so Teams, Zoom and the browser
  in the session see both (a microphone passed as a USB device stays outside the remote session). Keyboards, mice,
  touch screens, hubs and network adapters stay local; smart card readers go through the smart card channel.
  Touch screens work as touch in Windows. With `USB_MODE=disks` USB sticks stay on the thin client and appear in
  Windows as drives; with `USB_MODE=auto` the thin client decides device by device: a stick as a drive, a device
  with storage and something else (an instrument, a key with its own driver) whole.
- **Managed from a shared folder (SMB) with a Windows manager**, no server: the whole fleet in one window, settings
  for all devices or one, and the **remote screen** of any device ([the manager](#the-manager-the-whole-fleet-from-one-window)).
- **Signed updates** that never interrupt a session: from GitHub releases (checked every 3 hours, installed in
  the background, applied when the session is over), or from your folder when you decide.
  **Try a version on a few devices first**, and **go back** to an earlier one when something breaks
  ([`UPDATE_TO`](docs/configuration.md#management)): FreeRDP goes back with it.
  Debian security updates install by themselves.
- **Settings dialog on the device** (optionally behind a PIN): broker or PC, network (DHCP, static, Wi-Fi),
  management folder and its account, USB mode, web button, power schedule, language. A new device names itself
  from its network card (`thinclient-1a2b3c`).
- **Hardware test**: started by itself on the live system and from Diagnostics on any device, it checks processor,
  memory, disk, graphics driver, missing firmware, network, sound, USB, TPM, Secure Boot and the remote desktop, and
  can open a ready-made hardware report on GitHub (no name, address or serial number in it).
- **Diagnostics for the help desk**, no PIN needed (the ℹ button): network, can each broker or PC be reached,
  time, management folder, last events. Read only.
- **Locked down**: no desktop, no menus, no text consoles (Ctrl+Alt+F1..F12 do nothing), no password-less
  account.
- **Several monitors** become one remote desktop spanning all of them (`MULTIMON`).
- **Power schedule and Wake-on-LAN**, screen always on, monitors switched on late handled.
- **Web button**: a web app, free browsing, or a full screen kiosk page, with Chromium
  ([screens that only show a web page](#screens-that-only-show-a-web-page)).
- English, Italian and Dutch interface; more languages are one file each.

## The manager: the whole fleet from one window

`OpenThinRDP-Manager` is one PowerShell script for Windows 10/11 (English and Italian, nothing to install) that works
on the shared folder the devices report to. No server, no agent, no database: what you see is the files in the folder.

<p align="center">
<img src="docs/screenshots/manager-devices.png" alt="Manager: every device, its state, user and version, and its settings" width="49%">
<img src="docs/screenshots/manager-updates.png" alt="Manager, Updates page: all devices on one version, a pilot device on the newest" width="49%">
<img src="docs/screenshots/manager-health.png" alt="Health Center: hosts, cluster, VMs, domain controllers, SQL and backups in one tree" width="49%">
<img src="docs/screenshots/manager-desktops.png" alt="Desktops: who cannot sign in now and why, with brokers and Hyper-V hosts" width="49%">
</p>

- **Every device at a glance**: state, user, version, last report, a readable summary and the event log of each.
- **Power and commands**: power on with Wake-on-LAN, restart, switch off, send its status now, run a command and see
  its output.
- **Zero-touch from the domain**: *Name it in the domain* and a new device needs only a domain account; *Move the
  folder* moves the whole fleet to a new share in one step; *Check permissions* gives the devices' account exactly
  the rights it needs.
- **The configuration as text** too: `common.conf` and each device's file, checked like the pages before saving.
- **Settings for all devices or one**, checked before saving, with the value in use on each device and what is
  still on its way.
- **A new version on a few devices first, then on all**: *Release from GitHub* asks *pilot devices only* or *all
  devices*; the others stay where they are until *Release to all devices*.
- **Back to an earlier version when something breaks**, for the whole fleet or one device, FreeRDP included: one
  click on the Updates page.
- **Remote screen** of any device in your browser, over SSH only, with a notice on the device.
- **The Windows side of the desktops** (Remote Desktop Services with Hyper-V): who cannot sign in now and why, each
  user with the device, the desktop, its host, the session and the last sign-in; brokers and hosts checked (a broker
  that fails every request, a missing permission, a stuck RDVH agent), each problem with its fix; actions on VMs and
  sessions, always confirmed and logged.
- **Health Center: the health of the whole Hyper-V and RDS infrastructure from the manager**: hosts, failover cluster,
  storage, VMs, domain controllers, DNS, SQL AlwaysOn, the NAS and the witness, the backups, in one tree with a state
  for each item and a plain sentence for each problem; *diagnosis only* or *diagnosis and repair*, where only safe
  repairs run by themselves.
- **The history of the fleet**, problems grouped from every event log; a **vault** for the SSH key and the signing key; your
  fleet on **its own signing key**; logo and background; and the manager **updates itself** from the signed releases.

**Everything it does, page by page, with the steps for a pilot group and for going back: [docs/manager.md](docs/manager.md).**

## Screens that only show a web page

The same image runs the screens that never need a Windows desktop: a TV in the hall, a dashboard in the
office, an info point, a board in production. With `WEB_BUTTON=kiosk` and `KIOSK_URL`:

- At power on the page opens **full screen in Chromium**: no sign-in, no desktop, no menus, no address bar.
- The page is set **centrally**, for every screen (`config\common.conf`), a group or a single one
  (`config\<hostname>.conf`) in the management folder. Change it and each screen picks it up within a few
  minutes and reopens the page, without a restart.
- It **reloads itself** every `KIOSK_RELOAD_MIN` minutes when nobody is touching it, so a page that went to an
  error after a network glitch comes back by itself.
- The **power schedule** switches the screens on and off (`POWER_ON_TIME`, `POWER_OFF_TIME`, `POWER_ON_DAYS`),
  on cable or Wi-Fi; status and events of every screen are in the management folder like any other device.
- Cookies and saved sign-ins stay across restarts. For dashboards behind a login, a link with an access token
  (offered by most dashboard tools) avoids signing in on the screen at all.
- Someone at the screen can still reach the sign-in form: it shows for 5 seconds before the page, and
  Ctrl+Shift+W closes the page. The settings can be locked with a PIN.

Settings: [docs/configuration.md](docs/configuration.md#web-button-and-kiosk-page).

## Why it is built this way

**Why FreeRDP is not updated automatically.** Debian security updates install by themselves, but FreeRDP is
excluded. First, the image ships its own FreeRDP build with UDP, which Debian's packages would replace with a
version without it. Second, the remote desktop client is the part users depend on: a new FreeRDP version can
change how sessions, USB devices, smart cards or the graphics behave, and on a fleet a regression stops everyone
at the same moment. So FreeRDP comes with OpenThinRDP releases, after testing on real devices, and you can still
keep it as it is on one device (`/etc/openthinrdp/freerdp-pinned`).

**Why UDP on by default.** Over TCP, a busy server or a lossy line makes the screen fall behind; over UDP, Windows
lowers quality instead. The transport is now part of FreeRDP ([#13608](https://github.com/FreeRDP/FreeRDP/pull/13608),
merged after weeks of tests on our fleet), switched off there by default; OpenThinRDP switches it on, and
`TRANSPORT=tcp` is one setting away.

**Why a shared folder instead of a management server.** Every Windows network already has a file share and
someone who can manage permissions on it. The devices only read and write files there, so there is nothing to
install, patch or license on the server side, and the settings are plain text files you can read, diff and back
up.

**Why Debian.** Stable, security updates for years, every driver and firmware package, and a kiosk on top of it
that you can read: the whole client side is a few shell scripts in `rootfs/opt/openthinrdp`.

## How it compares

| | **OpenThinRDP** | Dell ThinOS | IGEL OS | Stratodesk NoTouch | ThinStation |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cost | free | comes with Dell thin clients | subscription per device | licence per device | free |
| Source | open (GPLv3) | closed | closed | closed | open |
| Runs on | x86-64 PCs and thin clients, UEFI or BIOS; Raspberry Pi 4 (experimental) | Dell thin clients | many x86-64 devices | x86-64 PCs, Raspberry Pi | x86 PCs |
| Protocols | RDP only | Citrix, Omnissa/VMware, Microsoft and more | Citrix, Omnissa/VMware, Microsoft and more | many | many (you build the image) |
| Management | shared folder + Windows tool, no server | Wyse Management Suite | UMS server | NoTouch Center | configuration files on a network server |
| Updates | signed, from GitHub or your folder | vendor firmware | vendor | vendor | rebuild the image |
| Install | ISO, live or automatic installation | preinstalled | installer or preinstalled | installer | build, then PXE or USB |

If you need Citrix or Horizon, vendor support or certified hardware, the commercial systems are the right
choice. OpenThinRDP is for networks built on Windows Remote Desktop that want a free, open client that is simple
to manage, and for anyone who wants to put FreeRDP's UDP transport to work. Product names are trademarks of
their owners; the comparison reflects public information and our understanding, corrections are welcome.

Each of them in more detail, and **Linux Mint or Ubuntu with Remmina**: [docs/alternatives.md](docs/alternatives.md).
Questions people ask first (hardware, drivers, UDP, Azure, PXE, 802.1X): [docs/faq.md](docs/faq.md).

## What comes next

Ideas we would like to build, roughly in this order. Tell us in an issue which ones you need, or send a pull
request:

- **Network installation (PXE)** for many devices at once.
- **More tested hardware** and more languages (one file each).

## Build your own image

Your logo, your broker, your settings and keys built in (Linux with Docker or Podman):

```
cp -r image/site.example image/site      # then edit image/site/site.conf and build.conf, add your logo
image/build.sh
```

The result is `out/openthinrdp-<version>.iso`. See [docs/building.md](docs/building.md).

## Layout

| Folder | Content |
|---|---|
| `rootfs/` | everything installed on the thin client (`/opt/openthinrdp`, udev rules, systemd units) |
| `image/` | the ISO build (live-build in a container), the FreeRDP build and the example site folder |
| `management/windows/` | the Windows manager (PowerShell, no installation) |
| `management/publish/` | building and signing update packages |
| `tests/` | tests that run in a Debian container |

## Contributing

Issues and pull requests are welcome. Please describe the hardware and the Windows side (broker, session
host version) for anything related to connections or devices. See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) and the
[code of conduct](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md).

Security problems: please report them privately, see [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md).

# Getting started: from a USB stick to a managed fleet

Step by step, in the order that works: try it on one device, install it, then set up the management folder and the
manager, and from then on every new device needs only a domain account. About an hour for the whole path, most of
it on the Windows side.

**What you need**: a Windows Remote Desktop target (an RD Connection Broker with session hosts or a Hyper-V VDI
collection, or a single Windows PC or server), a domain account to sign in with, one 64-bit x86 PC or thin client
with 2 GB of RAM, and a USB stick.

## 1. Try it live (10 minutes, nothing installed)

1. Download `openthinrdp-<version>.iso` from the [latest release](https://github.com/OpenThinRdp/openthinrdp/releases/latest)
   and write it to a USB stick (Rufus in DD mode, balenaEtcher or `dd`).
2. Boot the device from the stick. The menu starts the live system after 10 seconds; it never writes to the disk.
3. The **hardware test** runs by itself: processor, memory, disk, graphics, firmware, network, sound, USB, TPM.
   Read it, and if you like, *Send to the OpenThinRDP project* opens a ready-made hardware report on GitHub that you
   send with your own account (nothing in it identifies the device or the network).
4. The settings open: set the **broker** (or the Windows PC) and the **domain** (its full DNS name, e.g.
   `example.local`). If your DHCP does not hand out the DNS servers of the domain, put your domain controllers in
   **Primary DNS** and **Secondary DNS**. Save, sign in with your own account: your Windows desktop opens.

Not working? *Diagnostics* (the ℹ button on the sign-in screen) shows what the device sees; the
[FAQ](../faq.md) has the common cases.

## 2. Install it (3 minutes)

Restart from the stick and choose **Install**: it shows the disk it will erase and asks before writing. It
installs on the first internal disk, never on a USB disk. For many devices, *Unattended install* skips the question.

## 3. The Windows side (once)

- **UDP**: nothing to install. The session hosts accept RDP over UDP by default; keep the Group Policy *Select RDP
  transport protocols* not configured or on "Use both UDP and TCP", and UDP port 3389 open towards the session hosts
  ([details](../udp.md#server-side)).
- **Outside the office**: an RD Gateway or a VPN ([configuration](../configuration.md#rd-gateway)).

## 4. The management folder (once)

1. Create a share on any file server, e.g. `\\fileserver\thinclients`.
2. Create a **domain account only for the devices**, e.g. `svc-thinclient`, never a person's account: every device
   keeps its password.
3. Permissions: the account reads the folder and writes only in `status\`; administrators have full control. The
   manager checks this and, after asking, sets it (step 5). The rules and why: [management.md](../management.md#account).

## 5. The manager (on your Windows PC)

1. Download `openthinrdp-manager-<version>.zip` from the
   [latest release](https://github.com/OpenThinRdp/openthinrdp/releases/latest) and unpack it where only
   administrators can write (a share works: everybody starts the same copy). It updates itself from then on.
2. Start `OpenThinRDP-Manager.vbs` and choose the management folder.
3. **Check permissions** (top bar): it lists what is wrong for the devices' account and offers to correct it.
4. **Settings > Devices**: the settings for every device, at least the **broker** and the **domain** (and the DNS
   servers if your DHCP does not give the domain's). Each one is checked before it is saved; *Edit as text...*
   shows the same file as plain text.
5. **Settings > Manager > Management folder > Name it in the domain**: as a domain administrator, this writes the
   folder for the devices' account in `\\<domain>\NETLOGON\OpenThinRDP\folders.conf`.
6. Optional: the **vault** (the key for the remote screen and for signing updates with your own key), logo and
   background, the **Health Center** for the servers behind the desktops ([manager.md](../manager.md)).

## 6. Every new device from now on

Install it (step 2). In the settings at the first start leave the **management folder empty** and fill in only the
**domain**, the **devices' account** and its **password** (and the DNS servers if your DHCP does not hand them out).
Within five minutes the device finds its folder in the domain, takes the broker and every other setting from
`common.conf`, and appears in the manager. Its event log says `management folder from the domain`.

## 7. Run it

- **Updates**: *Release from GitHub* in the manager, first on **pilot devices**, then *Release to all devices*;
  something broke, *go back* to the previous version in one click ([manager.md](../manager.md#updates-a-few-devices-first-then-all-and-back-when-something-breaks)).
- **Power and commands**: power on with Wake-on-LAN, restart, switch off or run a command on a device.
- **Moving the folder later**: *Settings > Manager > Move the folder...* moves the whole fleet in one step.

What is in production, what is only tested and what does not exist yet: [status.md](../status.md); production
readiness area by area: [maturity.md](../maturity.md).

---

<!-- https://github.com/OpenThinRdp/openthinrdp/blob/main/docs/faq.md -->

# Frequently asked questions

## The project

### What is OpenThinRDP?

An open source operating system for thin clients that connect to Windows with Remote Desktop: RDS session hosts,
VDI collections behind an RD Connection Broker, or any Windows PC with Remote Desktop on. It is Debian 13 with a
locked-down kiosk on FreeRDP, the RDP UDP transport built in, and a Windows manager that runs the whole fleet from a
shared folder.

### Is it free?

Yes. GPLv3 licence, no cost per device, no subscription, no account. The ISO and the signed updates are on
[GitHub](https://github.com/OpenThinRdp/openthinrdp/releases/latest).

### Is it not too young to use in production?

It is young as a public project (October 2026), but not as a system. It comes from the thin client fleet of a
company, where it replaced a commercial thin client OS. It runs there every day on 14 devices at desks, tills, a
laboratory and weighing stations, and every release reaches that fleet. On top of that:

- 170+ system tests run on every commit;
- every release is installed in QEMU/KVM with Secure Boot;
- UDP was tested for hours with packet loss, cut networks and killed clients.

What is in production, what is only tested and what is missing: [status.md](status.md).

### Who maintains it?

The IT team of the company where it runs in production, in the open on GitHub. Bug reports, test reports on other
hardware and pull requests are welcome.

## Hardware

### Which hardware does it run on?

Any 64-bit x86 PC or thin client with UEFI or a legacy BIOS, 2 GB of RAM and 8 GB of storage (none to run it live
from a USB stick). Tested: Dell OptiPlex 3000 Thin Client in production, QEMU/KVM with UEFI and with BIOS. Used thin
clients such as Dell Wyse 5070, HP t630 or Fujitsu Futro S740 meet the requirements. See [hardware.md](hardware.md),
and the guides [replacing Dell ThinOS](guides/replace-dell-thinos.md) and
[turning an old PC into a thin client](guides/old-pc-thin-client.md).

### Did it leave drivers out to be light?

No. The ISO has the complete Debian 13 kernel (Linux 6.12) with every driver, and every firmware package of Debian.
Whatever works with Debian 13, or with Ubuntu and Linux Mint of the same period, works here. It is light because it
runs no desktop.

### Does it run on Raspberry Pi or ARM?

Experimentally. There is an SD card image for the Raspberry Pi 4, tested in emulation but not yet on a real board
([the image](https://github.com/OpenThinRdp/openthinrdp/releases/tag/rpi-test-1), [what to check](arm.md)). The
Pi 5 is not supported yet.

### Does it run on old 32-bit thin clients?

No: Debian 13 no longer supports 32-bit only CPUs.

## Remote Desktop

### Does it really use RDP over UDP?

Yes. FreeRDP has no UDP transport in any release yet; OpenThinRDP ships FreeRDP with the pull request that adds it
([#13608](https://github.com/FreeRDP/FreeRDP/pull/13608)), which we test and report on. With `TRANSPORT=auto` the
session uses UDP, and TCP when UDP is blocked. On a line losing 50% of its packets it kept 19-21 frames per second,
where TCP was down to 0.6 at 20% ([udp.md](udp.md)).

### Which Windows can it connect to?

Windows RDS session hosts and VDI collections through an RD Connection Broker, or a single Windows PC or server with
Remote Desktop on (Pro, Enterprise, Server), on premises or in Azure, AWS or any cloud. Kerberos with NTLM as fallback,
RD Gateway, and its own WireGuard or OpenVPN for devices outside the office.

### Does it work with Azure Virtual Desktop or Windows 365?

Not yet: they need a Microsoft Entra ID sign-in and Microsoft's own gateway, which the kiosk does not do. An RDS
deployment or Windows virtual machines in Azure work, through an RD Gateway or a VPN
([desktops in the cloud](configuration.md#desktops-in-the-cloud)).

### Citrix or VMware/Omnissa Horizon?

No, OpenThinRDP is RDP only. For those, see [the alternatives](alternatives.md).

### Do webcams, headsets, USB keys and smart cards work?

Yes:

- Webcams through the RDP camera channel, and headsets through the RDP audio channels, so Teams, Zoom and the
  browser in the session see them.
- USB keys go to Windows as drives, or as whole devices: signature keys, tachograph keys and other special devices,
  also when plugged in during the session.
- Smart card readers through the smart card channel.

## Management

### Do I need a server to manage the devices?

No. The devices report to a shared folder (SMB) and read their settings from it; a PowerShell manager for Windows
shows the whole fleet, changes settings for all devices or one, and opens the screen of any device in your browser.
No agent, no database, no management server ([the manager](manager.md)).

### How are updates done? Can I go back?

OpenThinRDP updates come as signed packages, from GitHub or from your folder. They install in the background and
apply when the session is over. A new version can go to a few pilot devices first, then to all. If something breaks,
the whole fleet or one device goes back to the version before, FreeRDP included. Debian security updates install by
themselves.

### Is it secure?

- Updates are signed, and can be signed again with the key of your site only.
- No desktop, no terminal, no text consoles.
- SSH with keys only, off by default.
- The device secrets are sealed in the TPM when there is one.
- The keys of the fleet are kept in a vault with an access code.

See [security.md](security.md) and [SECURITY.md](../SECURITY.md).

### Does it boot over the network (PXE)?

Not yet. OpenThinRDP runs live from a USB stick or is installed, with an automatic installation for rollouts.
Network boot is considered for a later version.

### Does it support 802.1X?

Yes, since 0.2.1: 802.1X on the cable and WPA2/WPA3-Enterprise Wi-Fi, with PEAP (a domain or machine account)
or EAP-TLS (a certificate from your CA). The RADIUS server is checked against your CA before any password is sent,
and on a switch without 802.1X the device goes on by itself. Setup with Windows NPS or FreeRADIUS:
[802.1X and Wi-Fi Enterprise](configuration.md#8021x-and-wi-fi-enterprise).

### Why not just Linux Mint with Remmina?

The hardware support is the same, but Remmina has no RDP over UDP. A desktop also has to be locked down and set up
PC by PC, and its updates come without pilot devices or a way back. See
[the alternatives](alternatives.md#linux-mint-ubuntu-or-debian-with-remmina).

### How do I try it?

Write the ISO to a USB stick and start a PC from it: the live system writes nothing to the disk. Set the broker and
the domain, and sign in ([five minutes](../README.md#try-it-in-five-minutes)).

---

<!-- https://github.com/OpenThinRdp/openthinrdp/blob/main/docs/alternatives.md -->

# OpenThinRDP and the alternatives

What OpenThinRDP does differently from the other ways of turning PCs into Remote Desktop clients, and when another
choice is better. The facts about other products are public information as we understand it; corrections are
welcome in the [discussions](https://github.com/OpenThinRdp/openthinrdp/discussions).

- [Linux Mint, Ubuntu or Debian with Remmina](#linux-mint-ubuntu-or-debian-with-remmina)
- [IGEL OS](#igel-os)
- [Dell ThinOS](#dell-thinos)
- [Stratodesk NoTouch](#stratodesk-notouch)
- [ThinStation](#thinstation)
- [openthinclient](#openthinclient)
- [What only OpenThinRDP does](#what-only-openthinrdp-does)

## Linux Mint, Ubuntu or Debian with Remmina

A general desktop with Remmina, or with FreeRDP itself, is the usual free answer. It is a good one for a PC or two.
For a fleet of Remote Desktop clients, here is what it means.

**Hardware support is the same.** OpenThinRDP is Debian 13 with its complete kernel and every firmware package
([hardware](hardware.md#drivers-all-of-debians)). A device that works with Mint or Ubuntu of the same period works
with OpenThinRDP too. Neither side has a driver advantage.

**No RDP over UDP.** Remmina and the `xfreerdp` of the distributions use the distribution's FreeRDP. FreeRDP has no
UDP transport in any release yet: it is the pull request [#13608](https://github.com/FreeRDP/FreeRDP/pull/13608),
which OpenThinRDP builds and ships. So on a busy server, on Wi-Fi or through a VPN the session runs over TCP. On a
line that loses packets, TCP queues the screen while UDP keeps it moving ([the numbers](udp.md#on-a-lossy-line)).

**A desktop to lock down.** Users can open other programs, change the settings, fill the disk. Making it a kiosk is
your work: automatic sign-in, no terminal, no other applications, no text consoles, a session that comes back by
itself, a device that switches off when the session ends. OpenThinRDP is all of that out of the box.

**Each PC set up by hand.** There is nothing to see the state of the fleet, nothing that sets all devices or one
from one place, and no screen of a device from your desk. The [manager](manager.md) of OpenThinRDP does this from a
shared folder.

**Updates of a whole desktop.** The whole operating system updates, FreeRDP included, whenever the distribution
says so. OpenThinRDP updates come as one signed package that you can send to a few pilot devices first. If something
breaks you go back to the version before, for the whole fleet in one click. FreeRDP never changes behind your back
(Debian security updates still install by themselves).

**The details of a thin client**, which you would have to rebuild:
- the RD Connection Broker with its collection, fallback brokers, and Kerberos behind a shared broker name;
- reconnecting after a network drop, but not after a deliberate sign out;
- *Waiting for Windows* while the virtual machine restarts;
- which USB devices go to Windows whole and which as drives;
- webcams and headsets through the RDP channels, so that Teams sees them;
- smart card readers;
- a power schedule and Wake-on-LAN.

**When Mint is the better choice:** the user also needs local programs (a real desktop with a remote session now and
then), or there are one or two PCs and nobody to manage them.

## IGEL OS

A commercial thin client operating system with a subscription per device, managed by the IGEL UMS server. It runs on
many x86-64 devices, with certified hardware and vendor support, and connects with many protocols: Citrix, Omnissa
(VMware) Horizon, Microsoft AVD, Windows 365 and RDP.

**Better for:** Citrix or Horizon, Azure Virtual Desktop and Windows 365, support contracts. **OpenThinRDP is for:**
networks built on Windows Remote Desktop that do not want a cost per device or a management server.

## Dell ThinOS

The operating system of Dell (Wyse) thin clients, managed with Wyse Management Suite, with Citrix, Omnissa Horizon and
Microsoft clients. It runs only on Dell thin clients. OpenThinRDP runs on those same devices too: the production
fleet it comes from is Dell OptiPlex 3000 Thin Clients that ran ThinOS before. It also runs on any other PC.

**Better for:** a Dell-only fleet with Citrix or Horizon, under Dell support.

## Stratodesk NoTouch

A commercial thin client operating system with a licence per device, managed by NoTouch Center. It runs on x86-64
PCs and on Raspberry Pi, with many protocols. **Better for:** many protocols, Raspberry Pi today (OpenThinRDP's
Raspberry Pi support is [in preparation](https://github.com/OpenThinRdp/openthinrdp/issues/61)), vendor support.

## ThinStation

An open source, long-standing thin client toolkit. You build your own image with the protocols you need, and the
devices boot it over the network (PXE) or from a USB stick or disk; the settings are files on a network server.
**Better for:** network boot (OpenThinRDP has no PXE yet), protocols other than RDP, and very old or very small
devices. **OpenThinRDP gives you:**
- a ready image, installed or live;
- the RDP UDP transport;
- signed updates with pilot devices and going back;
- a Windows manager with the remote screen;
- the device secrets in the TPM.

## openthinclient

An open source thin client system (with a commercial offer) whose devices boot over the network from the
openthinclient server, managed from that server, with many protocols. OpenThinRDP is a different, unrelated project:
it is installed on each device or runs live, and needs no server. **Better for:** network boot from a central server,
protocols other than RDP.

## What only OpenThinRDP does

- **RDP over UDP with FreeRDP**, tested on lossy lines and in daily production
  ([udp.md](udp.md)). Over TCP a line losing 20% of its packets gave 0.6 frames per second; OpenThinRDP over UDP gave
  19-21 at 50%.
- **No server to manage the fleet:** a shared folder and a Windows manager. Settings for all devices or one, the
  remote screen over SSH, and the problems of every device read together.
- **Signed updates with pilot devices and going back**, from GitHub or from your folder, re-signed with your own key
  if you want.
- **Built from a fleet in production.** It runs every day on 14 thin clients at desks, tills, a laboratory and
  weighing stations ([status](status.md)), a fleet that left a commercial thin client OS for it.
- **Free and open** (GPLv3), with no cost per device.

---

<!-- https://github.com/OpenThinRdp/openthinrdp/blob/main/docs/hardware.md -->

# Hardware

## Drivers: all of Debian's

OpenThinRDP is light because it runs no desktop, not because drivers were left out. The downloadable ISO carries
the **complete Debian 13 kernel (Linux 6.12) with every driver module, and every firmware package Debian has**
(`firmware-linux-nonfree`, `firmware-realtek`, `firmware-iwlwifi`, `firmware-atheros`, `firmware-brcm80211`,
`firmware-mediatek`, `firmware-amd-graphics`, `firmware-intel-graphics`, `firmware-sof-signed` and the others: the
`FIRMWARE=all` build of [building.md](building.md)). A network card, Wi-Fi adapter or graphics chip that works with
Debian 13, or with the Ubuntu and Linux Mint releases of the same period, works the same here. Only an image you
build yourself with `FIRMWARE=thinclient` keeps just the usual thin client firmware, to save about 600 MB.

The quickest way to know: start the ISO **live** from a USB stick. Nothing is written to the disk, and the
diagnostics (ℹ on the sign-in screen) show the network card, the address and whether the brokers answer.

## Requirements

| | |
|---|---|
| CPU | 64-bit x86 (x86-64): Intel, AMD, VIA. 32-bit only CPUs cannot run Debian 13 |
| Firmware | UEFI, with or without Secure Boot, or a legacy BIOS |
| Memory | 2 GB |
| Storage | 8 GB to install; none to run it live from a USB stick |

## Tested

| Device | Firmware | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Dell OptiPlex 3000 Thin Client (Intel Pentium Silver/Celeron, eMMC, Realtek NIC, Intel Wi-Fi) | UEFI, Secure Boot | the production fleet: 14 devices, boot to sign-in form in about 6 s after the firmware |
| QEMU/KVM virtual machine (OVMF) | UEFI, Secure Boot | every release: live system, automatic and confirmed installation, first update |
| QEMU/KVM virtual machine (SeaBIOS) | legacy BIOS | live system and installation |

## Should work: models that meet the requirements

These are common used thin clients with a 64-bit CPU, 2 GB of RAM or more and 8 GB of storage or more. We have not
tested them: if you try one, a line in the [discussions](https://github.com/OpenThinRdp/openthinrdp/discussions/3)
(model, what works and what does not) moves it to the table above.

| Family | Examples |
|---|---|
| Dell Wyse | 3040, 5060, 5070, 5470 |
| HP | t520, t620, t630, t640, t540 |
| Fujitsu Futro | S740, S940, S920 |
| Lenovo, IGEL and others | ThinCentre M625q, IGEL UD3 (x86-64 models), any office mini PC |

Some of them ship with less storage than 8 GB in their smallest version: run them live from a USB stick or put in a
bigger module.

## Not supported

- **ARM** other than the Raspberry Pi 4 (the Raspberry Pi 5, ARM thin clients): not supported yet.
- **32-bit only** CPUs (older Atom and VIA models): Debian 13 no longer runs on them.

**Raspberry Pi 4** (arm64), experimental: an SD card image built by `image/build-rpi.sh`
([pre-release](https://github.com/OpenThinRdp/openthinrdp/releases/tag/rpi-test-1)), tested only in QEMU arm64
emulation, not yet on a real board. What is different from a PC and what to check on the first board: [arm.md](arm.md).

## Firmware settings (Dell)

- **Wake-on-LAN**: enable "Wake on LAN" and **disable "Deep Sleep Control"**. With deep sleep in S4/S5 the
  network card is off and the magic packet never arrives. The same setting blocks the RTC alarm used by
  `POWER_ON_TIME`.
- **USB boot** must be enabled to install from a stick (Integrated Devices).
- On Linux the settings can be changed without entering the setup screen, through `dell-wmi-sysman`
  (`/sys/class/firmware-attributes/dell-wmi-sysman/`), with the BIOS admin password if one is set.

## Monitors

- A monitor switched on after the thin client (or a slow HDMI/DisplayPort link) leaves X without an output:
  the kiosk checks every 2 s and enables it.
- Monitors with a built-in USB hub may expose a "Hub Controller" device: it is kept local.
- Touch monitors stay local and their touches go to Windows as real touch input (`+multitouch`).

## USB devices seen in the field

- Webcams with microphone (UVC + audio): camera through the RDP camera channel, microphone through the RDP audio
  channel (tested with an eMeet Nova and an HD Web Camera 05a3:9331 against Windows 11 and Zoom).
- Signature keys with smart card reader + storage: the reader goes through the smart card channel, the
  storage as a whole device.
- Composite devices that restart in another mode once they see a PC (e.g. tachograph download keys): passed
  with `/usb:auto`, so they are passed again after re-enumeration. Devices plugged in during the session are
  passed only with a FreeRDP that has the `filter:` option of the USB channel (merged upstream after 3.32.1);
  with older versions plug them in before signing in, or list them in `USB_REDIRECT`.
- USB network adapters are never passed (the device would lose its own network).

---

<!-- https://github.com/OpenThinRdp/openthinrdp/blob/main/docs/status.md -->

# Status: what you can deploy today

OpenThinRDP is numbered 0.x, but it is not a prototype: it runs a company's whole thin client fleet every day.
This page says what is used in production, what is available but not exercised by that fleet, and what does
not exist yet, so you know what to test before rolling it out.

Is it ready for your production? Area by area, with the evidence and what is still missing: [maturity.md](maturity.md).

## The production fleet

- **14 Dell OptiPlex 3000 Thin Clients** (BIOS 1.19 to 1.37) in offices, at the tills, in a laboratory and at
  weighing stations: 13 wired, one on **Wi-Fi** (a wall screen that shows a web page all day).
- **Windows 11 VDI on Hyper-V**: personal desktops behind two RD Connection Brokers (DNS round robin), plus a
  handful of session hosts.
- Every device was **converted in place** from the system it ran before, by an update package, with its settings
  carried over; none was reinstalled by hand.
- Updates reach them from the **management folder, signed with the key of the site**: the manager checks each GitHub
  release (project signature and hash) and signs it again with that key. Installed in the background during sessions
  and applied when the session is over. Until October 2026 the devices took the GitHub releases straight.

## In production every day

| Area | What |
|---|---|
| Sign-in | Kiosk sign-in screen, default user, two brokers with fallback, load balance info for VDI collections; **Kerberos with NTLM as fallback** behind the brokers' round-robin name; a session opened from another device is told apart from a VM shutdown |
| Transport | **RDP over UDP** (`TRANSPORT=auto`) with fallback to TCP; reconnection after network drops |
| Network | Wired (DHCP) and **Wi-Fi** (WPA2-PSK) |
| Web | **Web button** that opens the company portal (app mode, allowed sites only) on every device; a wall screen in **web kiosk** mode |
| USB | Whole-device redirection of signature keys and other special devices, also plugged in during the session |
| Meetings | Webcams through the RDP camera channel, microphones and speakers through the RDP audio channels |
| Smart cards | Readers through the smart card channel (pcscd) |
| Touch | Touch screens at the tills, as real touch in Windows |
| Management | Status and events of every device, central settings (common and per device), logo and background, Windows manager |
| Updates | Signed packages from the **management folder** with the **site key** (`UPDATE_FROM=share`, `UPDATE_KEY=site`), the GitHub releases checked and signed again by the manager; straight from GitHub (`UPDATE_FROM=github`) before. Debian security updates by themselves |
| Power | Shutdown at the end of the session, Wake-on-LAN (also from the BIOS), **power on and off on a schedule** (the wall screen: RTC wake alarm) |

## Available, not exercised by that fleet

These work in our tests (QEMU/KVM at every release, the system tests in `tests/`, a test device), but the
production fleet does not use them, so test them in your environment first:

- **ISO installation** on new hardware: live system and automatic installation, Secure Boot. Tested in QEMU/KVM
  with Secure Boot at every release; the fleet itself was converted in place, not installed from the ISO.
- Static addressing (the fleet uses DHCP).
- Web button in free browsing mode (`WEB_BUTTON=browser`).
- `RDP_CERT=verify` with your own certificate authority.
- Devices outside the office: the RD Gateway (`RDP_GATEWAY`), tested against a Windows Server RD Gateway, and the
  VPN (`VPN=wireguard|openvpn`), tested against WireGuard and OpenVPN servers (tunnel, routes, DNS, a refused
  password). No device of the fleet works outside the office yet.
- **A pilot group and going back** (`UPDATE_TO`): a version on a few devices first, the others kept where they are,
  and back to an earlier version with its FreeRDP. In the system tests (management folder and GitHub, going back with
  the packages of that version), new in 0.2.0.
- **The manager updating itself** from the signed releases, new in 0.2.0.
- **802.1X and WPA2/WPA3-Enterprise Wi-Fi** (PEAP, EAP-TLS): in the system tests and in a lab against hostapd and
  FreeRADIUS, new in 0.2.1; not yet on a real switch or with Windows NPS.
- **Desktops in the cloud** (Azure, AWS, any provider): the same RDP, through an RD Gateway or a VPN, but we have
  no cloud deployment to test on ([what to know](configuration.md#desktops-in-the-cloud)).
- **Raspberry Pi 4** (arm64), experimental: an SD card image
  ([pre-release](https://github.com/OpenThinRdp/openthinrdp/releases/tag/rpi-test-1)), tested only in QEMU arm64
  emulation, not yet on a real board ([what to check](arm.md)).

## Not available yet

- Citrix, VMware/Omnissa Horizon or any protocol other than RDP.
- Azure Virtual Desktop and Windows 365 (Microsoft Entra ID sign-in and Microsoft's gateway).
- The Raspberry Pi 5 and other ARM devices.
- Network boot (PXE).
- Disk encryption, signed central configuration.

Tell us what you need first in the [discussions](https://github.com/OpenThinRdp/openthinrdp/discussions).

## Tested hardware

| Device | Status |
|---|---|
| Dell OptiPlex 3000 Thin Client | production (14 devices, one of them on its built-in Wi-Fi) |
| QEMU/KVM, UEFI with Secure Boot | tested at every release |

Other x86-64 PCs and thin clients with UEFI should work: reports in the
[discussions](https://github.com/OpenThinRdp/openthinrdp/discussions) are very welcome.

## When something goes wrong

- **A device cannot reach the management folder.** It keeps the last settings it read (the last good
  configuration) and keeps working. The ℹ button of the sign-in screen shows the network and the reachability
  of the folder and of the brokers; the settings dialog (PIN) fixes the folder, user or password on the device.
- **An update is interrupted.** A package is checked (signature, hash, syntax of every script) before anything
  is touched; Shut down waits for a running install. If the power goes in the middle, the device installs the
  same package again at its next check, because its version is still the old one.
- **Going back.** Devices never install an older version. To go back, publish the older package again under a
  higher version number, or reinstall the device from the ISO: its settings come back from the management folder.
- **A device is stolen.** Rotate the management folder password (`MGMT_PASSWORD` in the central settings) and,
  if it had one, the password of the session user. See [security.md](security.md).

---

<!-- https://github.com/OpenThinRdp/openthinrdp/blob/main/docs/manager.md -->

# The OpenThinRDP manager

The manager is the one place where you run a fleet of OpenThinRDP devices: one PowerShell script for Windows 10/11,
in English and Italian, with nothing to install. It works on the shared folder the devices report to: no server,
no agent, no database. What you see is the files in that folder, and everything you change is a file in that
folder too, with a backup and a line in the change log.

<p align="center">
<img src="screenshots/manager-devices.png" alt="Devices page: every device with its state, user, version and last report; the selected device with its settings" width="100%">
</p>

- [What you need](#what-you-need)
- [Devices: the whole fleet at a glance](#devices-the-whole-fleet-at-a-glance)
- [Settings for all devices or one](#settings-for-all-devices-or-one)
- [Updates: a few devices first, then all, and back when something breaks](#updates-a-few-devices-first-then-all-and-back-when-something-breaks)
- [Remote screen](#remote-screen)
- [History: problems across the fleet](#history-problems-across-the-fleet)
- [Desktops, brokers and Hyper-V hosts](#desktops-brokers-and-hyper-v-hosts)
- [Health Center: the whole infrastructure](#health-center-the-whole-infrastructure)
- [Vault, keys and the site key](#vault-keys-and-the-site-key)
- [Logo, background, SSH keys, permissions](#logo-background-ssh-keys-permissions)
- [The manager updates itself](#the-manager-updates-itself)
- [Starting it, and the command line](#starting-it-and-the-command-line)

## What you need

- A **shared folder** (SMB) that the devices can read and write their status to: `\\fileserver\thinclients`. How
  to create it, its account and its permissions: [management.md](management.md#account).
- A **Windows 10 or 11 PC** of an administrator, with PowerShell 5.1 (it is part of Windows). For the remote screen,
  also the OpenSSH client of Windows (`ssh.exe`, usually there) and a browser.
- **The manager itself**: `openthinrdp-manager-<version>.zip` from the [latest release](https://github.com/OpenThinRdp/openthinrdp/releases/latest),
  unpacked into a folder only the administrators can write (a share works, so that everybody starts the same copy).
  From then on it [updates itself](#the-manager-updates-itself).
- The devices set to that folder: `MGMT_SHARE` in their settings dialog, or in the image you build.

Start `OpenThinRDP-Manager.vbs` (no console window) or `OpenThinRDP-Manager.cmd -Folder \\fileserver\thinclients`.

## Devices: the whole fleet at a glance

The **Devices** page lists every device that reports to the folder, with a coloured dot for its state, the user
signed in, the version it runs and its last report; the search box finds a device by name, address or user. Devices
report every 5 minutes and at boot, and the list refreshes itself every minute. A device that stopped reporting,
rejected the central settings or has a failed service stands out in its colour.

Select a device and its header shows its address, version, last report and user, with its actions: **Remote
screen**, **Logo and background...**, **Software version...**. Under it:

| Tab | What it shows |
|---|---|
| Settings | every setting: the value in use on the device, where it comes from, and the value you set for it |
| Summary | a readable report: session, transport in use (UDP or TCP), network and Wi-Fi, software and FreeRDP, the version it installs, security updates, management, secrets, uptime |
| Events | the event log of the device: sessions, drops with their cause, updates, settings applied or rejected |
| Full report | the status file as the device wrote it |

<p align="center">
<img src="screenshots/manager-pilot.png" alt="A pilot device: the list marks it (pilot), its summary says it installs the newest version" width="100%">
</p>

## Settings for all devices or one

**Settings > Devices** holds the settings for every device (`config\common.conf`); in a device's **Settings** tab, tick *Exception*
to give that device a value of its own (`config\<hostname>.conf`), which wins over the common one. **Edit as text...**
opens the same file as plain text, comments included: it is saved only after the same checks as the page, in the form
the page would write (a Wi-Fi passphrase becomes its key, a PIN its hash), with the previous file in `config\backup\`.
Passwords show as `********`: leave them to keep them. Every row shows:

- the value **in use on the device** (from its last report);
- **where it comes from**: the device itself, the common settings, or an exception for this device;
- in orange, ***on its way***: a value you saved that the device has not applied yet. It reads the folder every 5
  minutes; when it stays orange, the device has refused the settings (its state says so).

The help of the selected setting is in full under the list. Before saving, the manager checks every value with the
same rules as the devices (a device refuses a whole configuration with one wrong value), and before saving the
common settings it lists the devices that would refuse them. Every save keeps a copy of the file in
`config\backup\` and adds a line to `config\changes.log`.

<p align="center">
<img src="screenshots/manager-common.png" alt="Common settings: every setting with its value and the help of the selected one" width="100%">
</p>

All the settings: [configuration.md](configuration.md).

## Updates: a few devices first, then all, and back when something breaks

The **Updates** page shows the newest version in the folder, the version all devices are on, the pilot devices,
the devices kept on a version of their own, the versions you can choose, and what the devices run now.

<p align="center">
<img src="screenshots/manager-updates.png" alt="Updates page: newest published version, all devices on 0.2.0, one pilot device on the newest, the versions that can be chosen" width="100%">
</p>

Everything here is one setting, `UPDATE_TO`, written for you in the right file:

| `UPDATE_TO` | where | means |
|---|---|---|
| `latest` | `common.conf` | every device takes each new version as soon as it is in the folder (the default) |
| a version, e.g. `0.2.0` | `common.conf` | every device stays on that version, or **goes back** to it |
| `latest` | `<hostname>.conf` | a **pilot device**: it takes the newest version even while the others stay |
| a version | `<hostname>.conf` | that device stays on, or goes back to, its own version |

A device installs a version also when it is **older** than its own, FreeRDP included, and installs nothing newer
until the setting changes. As always, an update never interrupts a session: it is installed in the background and
applied when the session is over.

### Try a new version on a few devices

1. **Choose the pilots.** In the header of a device, **Software version...** > *pilot device*. Pick devices that
   look like the rest of the fleet (the same model, the same kind of user), and users who will tell you when
   something is odd. The list marks them *(pilot)*.
2. **Bring the new version in for the pilots only.** **Release from GitHub...** (top bar or Updates page) downloads
   the latest release, checks its project signature and hash, and asks: *all devices* or ***pilot devices only***.
   With pilot only, all the other devices are first kept on the version they have (`UPDATE_TO=<that version>` in
   `common.conf`), and only then the new version goes into the folder.
3. **Watch the pilots** for a few days: their **Summary** and **Events**, and the **History** page.

### Release it to the whole fleet

When the pilots are fine: **Updates > Release to all devices**. `common.conf` goes back to `UPDATE_TO=latest`
and every device takes the new version within 5 minutes, each one when its session is over.

### Something broke: go back

- **The whole fleet:** **Updates > Version for all devices...**, choose the version that worked (newest first, from
  `updates\versions\`). Every device goes back to it, FreeRDP included, and stays there.
- **One device:** **Software version...** in its header > *its own version*.
- **A version that is no longer in the folder:** **Version from GitHub...** fetches it (the release `v<version>`,
  with the same checks) into the folder, without changing what the others get.

When the fix is out, **Release from GitHub...** again, pilots first, and **Release to all devices**.

**Good to know**

- Devices go back only to **0.2.0 or later**: older versions do not know `UPDATE_TO`.
- Devices that still run a version **before 0.2.0** ignore `UPDATE_TO` and take the newest version in the folder.
  The manager names them before a pilot-only release: the first time, release 0.2.0 to all devices, or update those
  devices first.
- With `UPDATE_FROM=github` (no management folder for updates) the same setting works: the devices fetch the release
  `v<version>` from GitHub.
- Every published version keeps its signed index in `updates\versions\`; the newest 3 packages stay in the folder,
  plus every version a device is kept on. Details: [management.md](management.md#pilot-devices-and-going-back).

## Remote screen

**Remote screen**, in the header of a device, shows its screen in your browser and lets you use it: to see what a
user sees, or to sign in once to a web page on a screen with no keyboard.

<p align="center">
<img src="screenshots/remote-screen.png" alt="The screen of a device in the browser, with the notice the device shows" width="80%">
</p>

It goes **through SSH only**, with the key of the manager's vault and a one-time password: nothing new listens on
the network, and nothing is installed on your PC. The device shows *Remote assistance active* while it lasts and
records it in its events; it ends when you close the small window, or by itself after 2 hours. `REMOTE_SCREEN=off`
turns it off. How it works: [management.md](management.md#remote-screen).

## History: problems across the fleet

The **History** page reads the event logs of every device together, for today, 24 hours, 7 or 30 days, and groups
what went wrong: failed sign-ins (by broker), desktops that did not start, sessions dropped (by cause), sessions
taken over, UDP blocked, failed updates, rejected settings. Each line says how many times, on which devices, for
which users, first and last time. A line is orange when 3 or more devices had the same problem: that points at a
server or the network, not at a device. "Six devices could not reach the broker this morning" is one line instead
of six logs.

## Desktops: the Distribution view of the Health Center

When a user cannot sign in, the cause is often on the Windows side: a broker that fails every request, a host whose
RDVH agent is stuck, a desktop that is saved or off, a session left disconnected. The desktops are part of the
**Health Center**: *who cannot sign in now* opens its headline, each personal desktop (VM) in its tree shows the user,
the Windows session, the last sign-in and the thin client, with the actions on the session (*Shadow*, *Message*,
*Disconnect*, *Log off*) and *Personal desktop of the user*. The button **Distribution** on top of the Health Center
shows the whole deployment as one table, searchable: user, device, desktop, host, state of the VM, session, last
sign-in (**Health Center** goes back to the tree). It works with Remote Desktop Services and Hyper-V (personal
desktops, and session hosts when there are some).

<p align="center">
<img src="screenshots/manager-health-vm.png" alt="Health Center, a personal desktop selected: the user, the Windows session, the last sign-in, the thin client, every check with OK, and the session actions" width="100%">
</p>

<p align="center">
<img src="screenshots/manager-desktops.png" alt="Health Center, Distribution: one row per user with the device, the desktop, its host, the state of the VM, the session and the last sign-in" width="100%">
</p>

- **One row per user and device**: the device, the personal desktop (VM), its Hyper-V host, the state of the VM
  (running, off, saved, not responding), the Windows session (active, idle for how long, disconnected since when) and
  the last sign-in: when, through which broker, and whether it took a second try.
- **Who cannot sign in now** is on top, in red, and named in one line above the list with what stops them. A colour
  never comes alone: the state says it in words.
- **Select a row**: one sentence says what is wrong, then the desktop, the session, the device and the last sign-ins,
  each with the broker that served or refused it.
- **Its actions**: *Shadow* (the screen of the session, with the user's consent unless the policy of the desktop says
  otherwise), *Message...*, *Disconnect*, *Start VM*, *Restart VM*, *Desktop...* (the personal desktop of the user),
  *Log off*, *Shut down VM*. The same on the row with a right click or the menu key. A button that cannot be used now
  is grey, and its tooltip says why.
- **Filters and search**: problems only, signed in, disconnected, VM off or saved; a user, device, desktop or host.
- The brokers and hosts are read **in the background every 2 minutes** (and with *Refresh*); the page says when. A
  host that does not answer never holds the window.

### Brokers and hosts

The brokers, the shared name the devices use, and the Hyper-V hosts are items of the Health Center tree: one line per
problem, in one sentence and, when a safe fix exists, with its button; **Show all** adds the healthy ones. When all is
well it is one green line, *Brokers and hosts: all OK*. A right click on a broker or a host gives all its actions.

| It checks | Fix |
|---|---|
| **Each broker**: sign-ins received and failed since midnight (or since its service started), and the last ones. A broker that fails every request it receives is an error even when it receives few: users get in at the second try, through another broker, and nobody reports it. Its known signature (it presents itself to itself without the `$` of its computer account, event 4648 of `tssdis.exe`) is named | **Restart**: Tssdis, TScPubRPC and RDMS stop and start again, Tssdis first, with time limits, a hanging process is ended; then its Kerberos tickets are purged |
| Its services, also those stuck in *StopPending* | **Restart** |
| Its database (events 2048, 2072) | |
| The **self-repair** task (below) | **Install** |
| The broker in the AD group of the settings | **Add** |
| **The shared name** (`BROKER` of the devices): every broker behind it, every address answering on port 3389 | |
| **Each host**: every broker in *RDS Endpoint Servers*, *RDS Management Servers* and *Hyper-V Administrators*, directly or through a group (nested groups too). The RDVH agent moves between brokers by itself: a missing permission breaks one broker at random | **Repair**: the AD group of the settings (or the broker's computer account) into the groups that miss it, then the tickets of the brokers |
| *VmHostAgent* and *vmms* stuck, the RDVH agent attached to no broker or with no broker to attach to | **Unblock**: the service stops with a time limit, its process is ended if it hangs, it starts again |
| VMs with a vTPM that the cluster would **save** when it stops them (`OfflineAction` 1): they may not start again | **Correct**: `OfflineAction` 2, shut down |

### Safe by design

- Every action asks first, saying exactly what will happen and to whom (*Signed in there: alice. Her open programs
  close without saving*; for those, *No* is the default), and goes into `config\changes.log` like every other change.
- A broker is restarted only while another one is healthy, and never two at once; one action at a time.
- VMs are shut down (Windows closes inside them), **never saved** and never switched off; a VM of the cluster starts as
  a cluster role.
- What stops or ends something is not offered on data older than 5 minutes: *Refresh* first.
- `OTR_MANAGER_VDI_DRYRUN=1`: every action says what it would run, and runs nothing.

### What it needs

- The manager started as an account that administers the brokers and the Hyper-V hosts, with **WinRM** (port 5985)
  open from the PC to them. The sessions are read from the desktops as `quser` reads them (remote RPC, allowed on a
  Windows 10/11 desktop by `AllowRemoteRPC`); log off, disconnect and message fall back to WinRM on the desktop.
  Without the rights, the page says so in one sentence and the rest of the manager works as before.
- Nothing to configure in most cases: the brokers come from `BROKER` and `BROKER_FALLBACK` of the devices, the active
  management server of the deployment names the other brokers, the hosts and the desktops, the clusters name their
  nodes. **Settings...** on the page (kept for your account on your PC, not in the folder): the **AD group of the
  brokers** (the hosts give their permissions to it, never to single computers), more brokers or hosts if they are not
  found, or the page turned off.
- How it reads them, and why not the RemoteDesktop cmdlets (blind on any server but the active management server): the
  comments at the top of `management/windows/OtrVdi.ps1`.

### Broker self-repair

A broker can start failing every sign-in after it leaves and joins the farm again: it presents itself without the `$`,
falls back to NTLM, and every request ends with *access denied* (event 804, `0x80070005`) until its services start
again. `management/windows/rds/Broker-SelfRepair.ps1` does that by itself, as a scheduled task started by the event
of that fault, at most once every 15 minutes. *Install the broker self-repair* on a broker of the Health Center installs or updates it; by hand:
`Install-BrokerSelfRepair.ps1 -Broker rdcb1.example.com, rdcb2.example.com` (`-Remove` takes it away). A broker that
already has a self-repair task of its own is left as it is.

## Health Center: the whole infrastructure

The Distribution answers "who works where, and who cannot sign in". The **Health Center** looks one
step further, at what all of it stands on: the Hyper-V hosts and their failover cluster, the storage, the VMs, the
domain controllers, DNS, an SQL AlwaysOn group, the NAS or the witness, the backups. One page instead of Failover
Cluster Manager, Hyper-V Manager, Server Manager, SQL Server Management Studio and the event logs.

<p align="center">
<img src="screenshots/manager-health.png" alt="Health Center: on the left the tree of the infrastructure with a dot for each item, on the right the selected host with its facts, its checks and their Fix buttons" width="100%">
</p>

- **On the left a tree**: cluster, its hosts and their VMs (or *Hyper-V hosts* without a cluster); the domain with its
  DCs and DNS; the SQL listener with its replicas; *Remote Desktop* with the brokers; the devices; the backups. Each
  item has a dot and a word (*Saved with a vTPM*, *Free memory*, *to see: 3*), never the colour alone.
- **On the right the selected item**: what is wrong in one sentence, then **every check it ran with its result**
  (*OK*, *Warning*, *Problem*, each with one short line: *Memory: 41% free*, *Clock: 0.2 s from the domain time*), its facts (up since, Windows, memory, disks,
  clock, addresses, VMs...), its checks (each: what is wrong, with its numbers, and what it means in plain words) with a
  **Fix** button where a fix exists, and its actions (*Drain the node*, *Resume the node*, *Start VM*, *Restart VM*,
  *Shut down VM*, *Move all VMs to the other node*, *Restart the server*, *Shut down the server*, *Resynchronise the
  clock*, *Replicate now*, *Wake up*, *Local administrator password (LAPS)*, and on a personal desktop the session
  actions...). A button that cannot be used now is grey and its tooltip says why.
- **On top** the headline (*Everything OK: 2 hosts, 16 VMs, 2 domain controllers*, or the problems), when it was read,
  and the mode. Read in the background every 3 minutes from the start: the menu shows the count of problems on any page.
- **With the desktops**: the findings of the brokers and hosts show up on the same items (read once, fixed the same
  way); a broker or a host has the actions of the desktops too (restart its services, empty its tickets, install the
  self-repair, unblock the RDVH agent, repair the permissions of the brokers).

<p align="center">
<img src="screenshots/manager-health-cluster.png" alt="Health Center, the cluster selected: nodes, witness, shared volume, storage pool, live migration, the VMs with a vTPM it would save and the room left if a node fails" width="100%">
</p>

### What it checks

| Item | Checks |
|---|---|
| **Every server** (host, DC, broker, SQL replica) | free memory and disk, services stuck in *StopPending*/*StartPending*, automatic services stopped with an error, a restart pending (updates), critical events and errors of the last day, the clock against the PDC emulator (SNTP) and where it takes its time from, the secure channel with the domain, active adapters with a 169.254 address |
| **Hyper-V host** | `vmms`, the cluster service, the RDVH agent (when the Desktops page does not watch it), its state in the cluster (up, paused, down), the guardian keys a VM with a vTPM needs on every node |
| **Cluster** | nodes up, the witness online (and its share answering), roles and resources failed, CSVs online and their free space, the storage pool, virtual and physical disks (disks in maintenance while a node is paused are said so), storage repair jobs, cluster networks and the ones live migration may use, *DrainOnShutdown*, VMs with a vTPM it would **save** (`OfflineAction` 1), room on the other nodes for the VMs of each node |
| **VM** | state, heartbeat (not responding), saved (a problem with a vTPM), paused, a running VM whose cluster role is offline (not watched), not a role of the cluster, checkpoints older than 3 days, the stop action of a VM outside a cluster, the disks inside when it answers WinRM by its name |
| **Domain and DCs** | the domain ports from this PC (LDAP, Kerberos, DNS, SMB, global catalog, ADWS), the DC services and their start mode (a *disabled* one is said so), SYSVOL and NETLOGON, inbound replication, the owners of the FSMO roles answering, 127.0.0.1 first in the DNS servers of a DC, the DCs alike (services, DNS zones) |
| **DNS** | every DNS server answers and how fast, every server name resolves to one address of its own and back (a storage or APIPA address registered under the name is the classic way of losing seconds at every connection), reverse lookups that are slow, reverse zones for the networks of the servers |
| **SQL AlwaysOn** (when configured) | the listener and the primary, every replica connected and healthy, every database synchronized (or synchronizing on an asynchronous replica) and not suspended, the SQL services of every replica, the same active logins and SQL Agent jobs on every replica (AlwaysOn copies databases, not logins), failed jobs of the last 3 days, Windows-only authentication on one replica, the last full backup of every database |
| **Hyper-V host, more** | network adapters (up, speed, driver and its date; a driver different from the other node is said), the UPS or battery when Windows sees one (on battery = a problem), the cluster volumes reachable from this node, the vTPM guardian keys |
| **Remote Desktop Gateway, RD Web** (on any server that has them) | the gateway service, its certificate (found, expired, expiring in 30 days), at least one connection and one resource authorization policy, port 443 answering, the failed connections of the last 24 hours; RD Web: the web server running |
| **Devices** | ping, the TCP ports given, an SMB share, Wake-on-LAN; a device that is the file share witness of a cluster says so, and the state of the witness |
| **Custom checks** | your own scripts, on the servers you choose (below) |
| **Backups** (when configured) | the newest file of a log folder, or the newest one with the text of a success, not older than the hours given |

### Diagnosis only, or diagnosis and repair

The **Mode** on top is for the page; **This item** on the right changes one item and what is under it (a cluster and
its hosts, the domain and its DCs). In *Diagnosis only* nothing is changed without a click and a confirmation. In
*Diagnosis and repair* the **safe** repairs of the items in that mode run by themselves after each reading, one after
the other, and each goes into `config\changes.log` (`health: automatic repair: ...: done`); the headline says what was
repaired last. A repair that was tried waits 30 minutes before it is tried again.

| Safe: runs by itself in repair mode | Always asks |
|---|---|
| Start a service a role needs (`vmms`, the RDVH agent, the cluster service, the DC services, the SQL services of a replica), unless it is **disabled** | Start a disabled service (someone may have disabled it on purpose), or another automatic service that stopped |
| Unblock `vmms`, the RDVH agent or the time service stuck in *StopPending*: stopped with a time limit, its process ended, started again (never `Restart-Service`, which waits for ever) | Unblock any other service; a service of a DC only while another DC is healthy |
| Resynchronise a clock; restart Netlogon when the secure channel is broken | Take the time from the domain again (`w32tm /config /syncfromflags:domhier`) |
| Bring the witness online | Start a failed cluster role; *DrainOnShutdown* = 1 |
| `OfflineAction` 2 for VMs with a vTPM (nothing running is touched) | Drain a node, resume it |
| Wake-on-LAN of a device that does not answer | Start, restart, shut down or resume a VM; bring its cluster role online; remove its old checkpoints; its stop action |
| The safe fixes of the Desktops page: restart the services of a broker (only while another broker is healthy), repair the permissions of the brokers on a host, unblock the RDVH agent | Replicate AD now; create a reverse DNS zone; resume the data movement of a database |

Never, by hand or by itself: a VM saved or switched off (a VM is shut down, Windows closes inside it), two DCs, two SQL
replicas or two brokers acted on within 10 minutes, SQL Server ended or failed over, a server restarted. **Drain the
node** refuses while another node is not up, the witness is not online (or a two-node cluster has none), a storage
repair runs, or the other nodes have not the memory for its VMs: then it moves them live and pauses the node, which can
be restarted; **Resume** puts it back with its VMs. One action at a time on both pages; what stops something is not
offered on data older than 5 minutes; `OTR_MANAGER_VDI_DRYRUN=1` makes every action say what it would run.

### Settings and what it needs

**Settings > Health Center** (the menu entry *Settings*), kept for your account on your PC (`%APPDATA%\OpenThinRDP\manager.json`), not in the
folder. **Nothing is found by itself**: servers can be on other networks or anywhere, so every server is entered by its
role, one list each, with a note for you (a name, a full name or an IPv4 address; a new line at the bottom of a list
adds, *Remove* removes):

- **Hyper-V hosts**, and whether they are in a **failover cluster** (*yes* with the name of the cluster: its other
